source.version: Published ACM version of record, Mensch und Computer 2025 (MuC '25), August 31-September 03, 2025, Chemnitz, Germany, pp. 407-421, DOI 10.1145/3743049.3743073 (p. 407 footer)
source.title_on_document: Groups and AI: How Access to Generative AI Influences Creative Teamwork

supplement.where: The paper refers to no external supplement. Appendix A (user creations, pp. 415-420) and Appendix B (Study 1 questionnaire ratings, Figure 4, p. 421) are inside this PDF.
supplement.holds: Nothing outside this PDF. No table of means, SDs, or test statistics beyond the F, Z, and p values in Section 4.1 (p. 410) and bar charts in Figures 2-4.

paper_design_summary: Study 1: 18 people in six groups of three did two creative marketing-campaign tasks (name, slogan, selling points, pen-and-paper sketch of product and logo), once with ChatGPT-4o and once with only Google search; order of conditions and products was counterbalanced, not stated as randomized. Participants rated their own group's result and process. Study 2: 20 external raters, blind to condition, rated and ranked the 12 resulting campaigns on items from the Creative Product Semantic Scale.

studies.label: Study 1 lab study (team marketing-campaign ideation, AI vs Google search), with the outputs rated by externals in Study 2

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the two conditions (AI: ChatGPT-4o; No AI: Google search without AI functionality) and pairing with the two products, counterbalanced across the six groups; every group did both conditions
assignment.quote: The order of conditions and products was counterbalanced across 6 trials, ensuring that each combination was used once.

arms.name: AI
arms.description: Group had access to ChatGPT-4o on a 55-inch shared screen during the ~20-minute campaign task

arms.name: No AI
arms.description: Group had access only to the Google search engine without AI functionality during the ~20-minute campaign task

participants.exclusions: None reported. 18 people in 6 groups of three (6 groups stated on p. 413, Conclusion); each person served in both conditions. The 20 external raters of Study 2 are raters, not participants who received AI help.
participants.who: Convenience sample in a university context, aged 20 to 29 (mean 25.6), computer science most common background, all had used AI tools before; student status not stated. Not compensated.
participants.country: Not stated; authors at RWTH Aachen University, Germany; study conducted in English
participants.quote: 18 people (9 male, 9 female) aged 20 to 29 years (mean = 25.6, SD = 2.7) participated in Study 1.

ai_tool.how_used: Groups freely prompted ChatGPT for names, slogans, and selling points and most also generated images (at least five per session) that they then copied into their hand drawing (pp. 410, 412)

task.description: Ideate a marketing campaign for a fictitious product (Glow-in-the-dark Umbrella or Smart Plant Pot): name the product, create a slogan, give 2-3 core selling points, and sketch product and logo with pen and paper
task.duration: Each condition designed to take approximately 20 minutes (p. 409)

outcomes.name: External rating: Conventional/Original (Creative Product Semantic Scale item)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Study 2: 20 external online raters (7 male, 13 female, aged 18 to 53), blind to AI use, rated all 12 campaigns on a -2 to 2 bipolar item; campaign and result order randomized. Analysis: aligned-rank-transform ANOVA with Use of AI and Campaign factors.

contrasts.reported: No significant effect reported for originality (text lists significant effects only for Organized, Practicality, Appeal, Focus). Figure 2 Study 2 panel: AI bar slightly above No AI bar, with SD whiskers; no numbers printed.

outcomes.name: External rating: Predictable/Unexpected (Creative Product Semantic Scale item)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Study 2 external raters as in S1-O1; -2 to 2 bipolar item.

contrasts.reported: No significant effect reported. Figure 2 Study 2 panel: AI and No AI bars at about the same level; no numbers printed.

outcomes.name: External rating: Impractical/Practical (Creative Product Semantic Scale item)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Study 2 external raters as in S1-O1; -2 to 2 bipolar item.

contrasts.reported: Interaction of Use of AI and Campaign on Practicality F1,57=4.8, p ≤ 0.05; no main effect of Use of AI reported. Post-hoc: 'only showed higher ratings for the Smart Plant Pot for AI in comparison to No AI (p ≤ 0.05)' (stated jointly for Practicality and Appeal). Figure 2: AI bar above No AI bar.

outcomes.name: External rating: Disorganized/Organized (Creative Product Semantic Scale item)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Study 2 external raters as in S1-O1; -2 to 2 bipolar item on how organized the campaign is.

contrasts.reported: Effect of Use of AI F1,57=5.43, p ≤ 0.05; interaction Campaign x Use of AI F1,57=20.45, p ≤ 0.001. Post-hoc: Smart Plant Pot x AI significantly more organized than Smart Plant Pot x No AI and Glowing Umbrella x AI (p ≤ 0.05, Holm-corrected).

outcomes.name: External rating: Unappealing/Appealing (Creative Product Semantic Scale item)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Study 2 external raters as in S1-O1; -2 to 2 bipolar item on appeal.

contrasts.reported: Interaction of Use of AI and Campaign on Appeal F1,57=10.12, p ≤ 0.01; no main effect of Use of AI reported. Post-hoc: higher ratings for Smart Plant Pot for AI vs No AI (p ≤ 0.05) (stated jointly for Practicality and Appeal). Figure 2: AI bar above No AI bar.

outcomes.name: External rating: Unfocused/Well-defined (Creative Product Semantic Scale item, 'focus')
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Study 2 external raters as in S1-O1; -2 to 2 bipolar item on definition/focus.

contrasts.reported: Effect of Use of AI F1,57=4.38, p ≤ 0.05; interaction Use of AI x Campaign F1,57=7.47, p ≤ 0.01. Post-hoc: Smart Plant Pot x AI significantly more focused than Glowing Umbrella x AI and Smart Plant Pot x No AI (p ≤ 0.05).

outcomes.name: External preference ranking of the six results per campaign
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Study 2: 20 externals ranked the 6 results per campaign 'on their preference' (rank 1 best); frequencies of AI and No AI results per rank shown in Figure 3.

contrasts.reported: 'AI results were ranked slightly better.' 'Overall, the AI results were rated and ranked slightly better than the No AI results.' No test reported.

outcomes.name: Self-ratings of own group's result on the six Creative Product Semantic Scale items
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Study 1 participants rated their own group's campaign on the same six bipolar items (-2 to 2) after each condition; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Self-report, so it does not meet criterion 3.

contrasts.reported: Only significant Study 1 effect was cognitive effort (Z = -3.18, p ≤ 0.01; AI mean = -0.56, SD = 0.78 vs No AI mean = 0.33, SD = 0.84), a process measure; 'No other significant effects were found.' Figure 2 Study 1 panel shows the six items without numbers.

outcomes.name: Self-reported preference and perceived creativity of results across conditions
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Final questionnaire: which campaign participants preferred and written justifications. Self-report; does not meet criterion 3.

contrasts.reported: Preference: 7 preferred AI, 4 No AI, 7 no clear preference. 'Most of the participants felt like the group produced more creative results when using No AI, while only 4 felt that their AI-assisted results were more creative.'

company_involvement.description: Funded in part by the German B-IT Foundation; no company involvement stated.

eligibility.reason: Within-group crossover with counterbalanced (not stated as randomized) order of AI and No AI conditions across 6 groups. Only 18 participants (6 teams of three) produced the outputs, far below 50; the 20 Study 2 people are raters, not treated participants. External blind ratings of the outputs satisfy criterion 3. Fails criterion 2 (p. 409, Section 3.1).

one_line_finding: With 6 teams of three (18 people), 20 blind external raters rated ChatGPT-assisted campaigns as more organized (F1,57=5.43, p ≤ 0.05) and better defined (F1,57=4.38, p ≤ 0.05) and ranked them slightly better, with no significant difference reported on originality; participants' self-ratings showed no significant differences (p. 410, Section 4.1; Figures 2-3).
open_questions: Whether a counterbalanced (not stated as randomized) crossover order satisfies criterion 1; moot here because the study fails criterion 2.
The paper's 'Study 2' is a rating study of Study 1's outputs; this form codes it as outcomes of S1 rather than as a separate study. The other screener may code it as S2.
Number of ratings behind the F1,57 tests is not stated; 20 raters x 12 campaigns would be 240 ratings per item, but the paper does not print this.
Population code: university convenience sample, student status not stated; coded 'mixed'.
notes: Outputs are 12 campaigns (6 groups x 2 conditions), shown in Appendix A (pp. 415-420). Directions for S1-O1 and S1-O2 come from reading the Study 2 bars in Figure 2; no numbers are printed. Not listed as outcomes: process measures (Team Effectiveness items, NASA-TLX, 'I felt inspired', collaboration quality; Appendix B Figure 4, p. 421) and qualitative reflexive thematic analysis of video recordings (Section 4.2, pp. 410-412), which are not scored on the output. No diversity or homogenization outcome.
